documents.title: Why the four-day week stalled in the public sector
documents.text:
When the council of a mid-sized northern town announced a trial of a four-day week for its administrative staff, supporters predicted a wave of imitators. Eighteen months later, only two other authorities have followed, and the original trial has quietly been extended rather than made permanent.

The disappointment is instructive. Productivity, which critics had feared would fall, held steady in nearly every department, and sick leave declined by almost a fifth. The difficulty lay elsewhere. Unlike a software firm, a council cannot simply close its doors on Fridays: residents expect the housing office and the registry to be open, so managers had to stagger staff rotas, which in practice meant that many employees worked longer days to compress their hours. Several said they felt more tired, not less, by Thursday afternoon.

Union representatives, initially enthusiastic, have grown cautious. They point out that the savings promised to taxpayers depend on the very efficiency gains that make staff reluctant to give up the extra day. "You cannot ask people to work faster and then tell them the reward is the same hours," said one organizer. The council's finance chief, meanwhile, insists the experiment has been worthwhile, if only because it has cut the cost of recruiting replacements for staff who might otherwise have left.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the article?
choices: Productivity fell sharply once the trial began
Unions have demanded a five-day week to return
The trial worked but proved hard to extend
Software firms are copying the council's example
questions.explanation: Results held steady, yet services needing weekday cover and tired staff limited the spread of the idea.

questions.prompt: What difficulty did managers face?
choices: Residents expect offices to stay open on Fridays
Staff refused to sign new contracts for Friday work
The registry lacked space for extra employees
Sick leave increased once rotas were staggered
questions.explanation: A council 'cannot simply close its doors on Fridays', so rotas had to be staggered.

questions.prompt: What does the organizer's remark suggest?
choices: Employees would accept longer weeks for more pay
The council has promised savings it cannot make
Taxpayers will refuse to fund additional leave
Efficiency gains may leave workers no better off
questions.explanation: Savings rely on faster work, yet the reward is only the same compressed hours.

questions.prompt: Why does the finance chief call the experiment worthwhile?
choices: Fines for late services have been reduced
Fewer staff may leave, so hiring costs are lower
The town received money from a national fund
Productivity improved in every single department
questions.explanation: It 'has cut the cost of recruiting replacements for staff who might otherwise have left'.

documents.title: Request to postpone the audit of the Tallinn facility
documents.text:
To: Ingrid Solheim, Head of Internal Audit
From: Dominik Farrar, Operations Director
Subject: Request to postpone the Tallinn audit

Dear Ingrid,

I am writing to ask whether the audit of the Tallinn facility, scheduled to begin on 12 March, could be moved to the week of 7 April. I appreciate that your team has planned its travel and that a postponement is never convenient, so let me explain why I think it is justified.

The facility is midway through the migration to the new warehouse management system, and the cutover is not due to finish until 28 March. An audit conducted now would therefore examine procedures that are about to be retired, as well as records that are temporarily held in two separate systems. I suspect your auditors would spend most of their time reconciling data that will be cleaned up within a month, and the findings would be of little use to either of us.

I recognize that you may be reluctant to reschedule, given that the audit plan was approved by the board. For that reason I would not object if the preliminary stage, the review of safety documentation, went ahead on the original date, since that work does not depend on the new system. Please let me know whether this compromise would be acceptable.

With thanks,
Dominik

questions.prompt: Why is Mr. Farrar writing to Ms. Solheim?
choices: To report several errors found in the Tallinn records
To ask for a change in the date of an inspection
To cancel the audit plan approved by the board
To invite her team to test the new system
questions.explanation: He asks to move the audit from 12 March to the week of 7 April.

questions.prompt: According to the email, what would the auditors waste time on?
choices: Travelling between two different warehouses in Tallinn
Reviewing safety documents that are out of date
Training staff in the new management system
Matching data that exists in two systems at once
questions.explanation: Records are 'temporarily held in two separate systems' and would need reconciling.

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Farrar imply about the board's approval?
choices: It makes Ms. Solheim unlikely to move the dates
It covers only the safety documentation review
It was given before the new system was chosen at all
It forbids any partial audit from going ahead
questions.explanation: He recognizes she 'may be reluctant to reschedule' because the plan was approved.

questions.prompt: What compromise does he offer?
choices: Auditing only the new system, in March itself
Sending the board a full preliminary report
Reviewing the safety papers on the first date
Moving the whole audit to the main office
questions.explanation: The preliminary safety review could go ahead on the original date.

documents.title: Notice to residents of Aldwych Terrace
documents.text:
NOTICE TO ALL RESIDENTS
Water supply interruption and parking restrictions

Wessex Water will carry out essential replacement of the main pipe beneath Aldwych Terrace between Monday 14 and Friday 18 October. Because the pipe lies directly under the carriageway, excavation will be required along the full length of the street, and the road will be closed to all vehicles from 7 a.m. each day.

Residents will experience two interruptions to their supply. The first, on Tuesday between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m., is needed to isolate the old pipe; the second, on Thursday afternoon, will allow the new main to be connected. The contractor expects each interruption to be shorter than announced, but cannot guarantee it. Households with a medical need for continuous water, including those using home dialysis equipment, should telephone the freephone number below by Friday 11 October so that alternative arrangements can be made.

Cars parked on Aldwych Terrace after midnight on Sunday will be moved at the owner's expense. Temporary permits for the Granger Street car park are available from the housing office on presentation of a vehicle registration document. Please note that, because of the size of the machinery, bins will be collected from the junction with Fenn Road throughout the week.

choices: To announce a permanent closure of the road
To ask residents to pay for a new water main
To invite residents to a meeting about parking
To warn residents of disruption from pipe work
questions.explanation: The notice describes road closure, two supply interruptions and parking and bin changes.

questions.prompt: Who must phone before 11 October?
choices: Residents who wish to buy a car park permit
Residents needing continuous water for health
Owners of cars parked after midnight on Sunday
Households that expect to be away all week
questions.explanation: Households with a medical need, such as home dialysis, should call by 11 October.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the Tuesday interruption?
choices: It will affect only the households on one side
It has been moved from the Thursday afternoon
It could end earlier than the stated four hours

questions.explanation: The contractor 'expects each interruption to be shorter than announced, but cannot guarantee it'.

questions.explanation: Bins will be collected from the junction with Fenn Road throughout the week, not from each house.

documents.title: A guidebook that rewards patience
documents.text:
Few travel guides dare to be as opinionated as The Slow Road to Anatolia, and fewer still manage to be as useful. The author, Selin Karaca, abandons the usual lists of top ten sights in favor of seven itineraries, each built around a single journey by train, ferry or bus, and she is frank that some of them demand more time than the average holiday allows.

The strongest chapters are those that depart from the obvious. Her account of a two-day rail crossing of the interior is exact about the timetable, the quality of the buffet car and the best seats from which to see the plateau at dusk, yet it never reads like a checklist. By contrast, the section on the coast is thinner, partly because the author confesses she dislikes crowded resorts and dismisses them in a few pages. Readers who plan to spend their time there will find less to guide them.

The maps are a weakness: printed in pale gray, they are hard to read in poor light, and several rural stations are marked with the wrong spelling. These are small flaws in a work of real character. It will not suit anyone who wants every hour planned in advance, but those prepared to trust a strong guide will be rewarded.

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer's overall opinion of the book?
choices: Admirable and distinctive, though uneven
Dull and badly organized from start to finish
Useful chiefly to those visiting the coast
Impressive because of its detailed maps
questions.explanation: The review praises its character and strongest chapters while noting a thin coastal section and poor maps.

questions.prompt: Why is the coastal section weaker?
choices: The coast can only be reached by an unreliable ferry
The rail timetable there is difficult to follow
The author prefers to avoid busy tourist resorts
The maps for that area contained too many errors
questions.explanation: The author 'dislikes crowded resorts and dismisses them in a few pages'.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the intended reader?
choices: A visitor with only a few days to spare in total
Someone willing to follow one writer's judgment
A traveler who wants to be driven everywhere
An expert who has already seen the plateau
questions.explanation: It will not suit those wanting every hour planned, but rewards those who 'trust a strong guide'; some trips need more time than a usual holiday.

questions.prompt: The word "exact" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
choices: demanding
expensive
hurried
precise
questions.explanation: Being exact about timetable and buffet car means giving precise detail.

documents.title: Guidance on handling confidential client documents
documents.text:
MEMO
To: All associates and trainees
From: Priya Venkataraman, Managing Partner
Subject: Guidance on confidential client documents

Over the past quarter, two incidents have prompted this reminder. In the first, a trainee left a folder of draft contracts on a train; in the second, a document intended for one client was attached to an email addressed to another, though the error was caught before it caused harm. Neither case involved bad faith, which is precisely why they deserve attention: carelessness, not malice, is the commonest source of a breach.

With immediate effect, documents marked "restricted" may not be taken out of the building in paper form, and may be sent electronically only through the firm's encrypted portal. Ordinary email may continue to be used for routine correspondence, but any attachment must be reviewed by a second person before it is sent to a client whose name appears on the sensitive-matters list. I recognize that the second check will cost a few minutes. I would argue that it costs less than the conversation we would have to have with a client after a mistake.

Associates are asked to remind trainees of these rules during their first week and to report any breach, however minor, to the compliance officer within 24 hours. Reports made promptly will be treated as an act of responsibility, not as an admission of fault.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the memo?
choices: To announce the dismissal of a careless trainee
To explain a change in the firm's encryption supplier
To tighten rules after two document-handling lapses
To introduce a new list of sensitive clients
questions.explanation: The memo follows two incidents and sets new restrictions on how documents move.

questions.prompt: What does the managing partner say about the incidents?
choices: They stemmed from inattention, not ill intent
They were deliberately staged to test the staff
They resulted in serious harm to one client
They were caused by faults in the encrypted portal
questions.explanation: Neither involved bad faith; carelessness is 'the commonest source of a breach'.

questions.prompt: What is required before an attachment goes to a sensitive-matters client?
choices: The compliance officer must approve it
It must be sent through ordinary email only
The client must sign a receipt
A colleague must look it over first
questions.explanation: Any such attachment 'must be reviewed by a second person before it is sent'.

questions.prompt: What does the final sentence suggest about reporting breaches?
choices: Minor breaches need not be reported
Prompt reporting will be viewed favorably
Reports must be made by the trainees themselves
Associates will be punished for any error
questions.explanation: Prompt reports 'will be treated as an act of responsibility, not as an admission of fault'.

documents.title: Head of Sustainability, Calder Packaging Group
documents.text:
Calder Packaging Group, a family-owned manufacturer with plants in four countries, is seeking a Head of Sustainability to lead a program that the board has described as the most consequential of the decade. We have committed to halving the carbon footprint of our products by 2032, and we need a leader who can turn that commitment into practice, plant by plant.

The successful candidate will report directly to the chief executive and will sit on the executive committee. You will build and manage a small team, negotiate with suppliers of recycled materials, and represent the group in discussions with regulators. Equally important, you will persuade production managers, many of whom have spent their careers prioritizing speed over everything else, that the new targets are achievable without ruining their margins.

We expect at least ten years of experience, of which five should have been in an industrial setting; academic credentials alone will not suffice. Fluency in English and one other European language is essential. Experience of reporting under recognized international standards will be an advantage, though we are more concerned with a record of changing how factories actually operate than with a long list of certificates.

The salary is competitive and reflects the seniority of the post. Applications, including a one-page statement describing a sustainability project you led and what you would do differently, should be sent by 30 June.

questions.prompt: What is the main challenge of the role?
choices: Raising money from investors for several new factories
Turning a company pledge into daily plant practice
Replacing the board with outside experts
Selling packaging to regulators in four countries
questions.explanation: The company wants someone to 'turn that commitment into practice, plant by plant'.

questions.prompt: What kind of resistance may the successful candidate meet?
choices: Suppliers who refuse to provide recycled materials

Regulators who oppose the footprint reduction

questions.explanation: Managers have 'spent their careers prioritizing speed over everything else'.

choices: Industry experience matters more than degrees

questions.explanation: Academic credentials alone will not suffice; the company cares more about changing how factories operate than certificates.

A short account of a project and a better approach
A certificate from an international standards body
questions.explanation: Applicants send a one-page statement about a project they led and what they would do differently.

documents.title: Messages between a project manager and a client
documents.text:
Hannah Roth [9:12]: Good morning, Mr. Eze. I wanted to let you know before the meeting that the contractor has found asbestos behind the kitchen wall. It was a precaution to test, but the result came back positive last night.

Obinna Eze [9:15]: That's very worrying. Does it mean the work stops?

Hannah Roth [9:17]: For the kitchen, yes, until a licensed team has removed it. The rest of the house is unaffected, so the electricians can continue upstairs. I've asked for a quotation, and the first indication is between 3,000 and 4,500 dollars, depending on how far it extends.

Obinna Eze [9:20]: That is well above the contingency we set aside, isn't it?

Hannah Roth [9:21]: It is, by about a thousand at the lower figure. Your insurer might cover part of it if the report shows that the material was undisturbed, but I wouldn't count on it.

Obinna Eze [9:24]: Understood. What would you recommend?

Hannah Roth [9:26]: Approve the removal now. Delay will cost more than it saves, because the plumber is booked only for the next three weeks. We can discuss the budget this afternoon.

Obinna Eze [9:27]: Fine. Send me the report and the quotation as soon as you have them.

documents.title: Frequently asked questions: the Meridian rail pass
documents.text:
The Meridian Pass allows unlimited travel on all regional services for a fixed period, but a number of conditions are worth understanding before you buy.

Can I use the pass on express services? Yes, although a seat reservation is compulsory on express trains and costs an additional fee. Pass holders who board an express without a reservation may be asked to pay the full fare, and the conductor has no discretion in this matter.

Does the pass start when I buy it? No. The pass is valid from the first date you choose, up to six months after purchase, and the period of validity begins only when you first travel. Please note that a pass whose start date has passed cannot be extended or refunded.

What if my train is cancelled? Pass holders are entitled to travel on the next available service, including a faster one, at no charge. If the delay exceeds ninety minutes, you may claim a voucher worth ten percent of the pass's daily value, though vouchers cannot be exchanged for cash.

Can the pass be shared? It cannot. Each pass is linked to the holder's passport number, which will be checked on board. Passes found to be in use by anyone other than the named holder will be confiscated without compensation.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the page?
choices: To explain the rules of a travel pass
To advertise a discount on express fares
To report on long delays in regional services
To compare the pass with a competitor's
questions.explanation: The page answers questions about conditions of the pass.

questions.prompt: When does the validity period begin?
choices: On the date the pass is purchased online
Six months after the pass is bought
When the holder first boards a train
When a seat has been reserved
questions.explanation: The period begins only when you first travel, within six months of purchase.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about a passenger on an express without a reservation?
choices: The conductor may let the passenger stay free
The conductor must charge the standard fare
The passenger will receive a voucher
The pass will be confiscated at once
questions.explanation: The conductor 'has no discretion', so the full fare may be demanded.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true?
choices: A cancelled train allows travel on a faster train

Late use of an expired start date is not refundable
A voucher can be cashed in after a long delay
questions.explanation: Vouchers 'cannot be exchanged for cash', so the statement that they can is false.

documents.title: Letter of recommendation for a research assistant
documents.text:
To the Selection Committee,

I am pleased to support Mr. Teodor Brandt's application for the doctoral fellowship. I supervised his master's thesis for two years and have since worked with him on a joint article, so I can speak with some authority about both his abilities and his limits.

Mr. Brandt's greatest strength is his refusal to accept an elegant explanation merely because it is elegant. When his early results on soil erosion appeared to confirm our hypothesis, it was he who proposed repeating the measurements at a second site, a decision that delayed his thesis by three months and, in the end, overturned the original finding. Few students of his age would have accepted such a setback with so little complaint.

I should add that he is not a natural presenter. His conference talks are accurate but dense, and he has yet to learn that an audience requires a story as well as data. I have no doubt that he will improve, as he has with every other aspect of his work once the problem was pointed out to him.

I recommend him without reservation. A fellowship would give him the freedom to pursue a question that matters, and I expect that the results will justify the committee's confidence.

Yours faithfully,
Prof. Alma Reinholt

documents.title: Cities weigh the cost of free public transit
documents.text:
When the city of Verhoeven abolished fares on its buses and trams two years ago, it hoped to cut congestion and help poorer residents reach work. The experiment has produced a surprising mixture of success and embarrassment.

Ridership rose by roughly a third, as expected, but a study by local researchers found that much of the increase came not from drivers leaving their cars, but from people who had previously walked or cycled. The reduction in traffic was therefore modest, a few percent at most. On the other hand, surveys show that low-income households have benefited considerably, with many reporting that they now travel to job interviews and clinics they would once have skipped.

The financial picture is complicated. Fares had covered less than a quarter of operating costs, so the loss of revenue was smaller than critics warned, yet crowding has forced the operator to buy additional vehicles, an expense no one had budgeted. Supporters argue that the real gain lies in what cannot easily be measured, such as lower collection costs and shorter boarding times. Skeptics respond that the same money, spent on more frequent services, might have persuaded more motorists to switch.

Other cities are watching closely. Several have said that they will wait for a third year of data before deciding.

questions.prompt: What does the article say about the effect on traffic?
choices: It increased because of crowding

It dropped by roughly a third in total
It could not be measured with any accuracy
questions.explanation: The reduction in traffic was 'modest, a few percent at most'.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the article?
choices: Free transit has failed on every test

questions.explanation: The article balances benefits for poor residents with modest traffic gains and unexpected costs.

choices: Many were not former car drivers

They were mainly tourists using the trams

questions.explanation: Much of the increase came from people who had previously walked or cycled.

choices: Fares should have covered all the operating costs

The money might be better spent on frequency
Cycling should be discouraged in city streets
questions.explanation: They argue that spending on more frequent services 'might have persuaded more motorists to switch'.
